title.en: Objectives of foreign policy, Panchsheel and Non-alignment

text.en: When India became free, the world was splitting into two armed camps led by the USA and the USSR. Nehru decided that the new nation would join neither and would speak with its own voice.

Foreign policy is a country's policy to protect and promote its national interests in dealings with other countries, bilaterally and multilaterally.
Article 51 of the Constitution sets directive principles: promote international peace and security, just relations, respect for international law, and settlement of disputes by arbitration.
The main tools are treaties, ambassadors, foreign aid, trade and armed forces, and the Ministry of External Affairs conducts relations.
The chief objectives are national security, national prosperity, more friendly nations, world peace and economic development.
The determinants include geography, history and traditions, natural resources, economic needs, political stability, military strength and the international milieu.
The 1950s and 1960s were the most idealistic phase under Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru.
Newly independent nations faced economic difficulty and pressure to align with the USA or the USSR.
Nehru chose non-alignment, not tying oneself to military blocs but judging issues independently and keeping friendly relations with all.
The term non-alignment was coined by V.K. Krishna Menon in his 1953 speech at the United Nations.
Panchsheel, the five principles of peaceful coexistence, was signed by Nehru and Chou En-lai of China on 28 April 1954 (the five principles are listed in a picture in the textbook).
These principles were incorporated in the Bandung Declaration of the Afro-Asian Conference in 1955 in Indonesia.
The Non-Aligned Movement was founded by Nehru, Tito of Yugoslavia, Nasser of Egypt, Sukarno of Indonesia and Nkrumah of Ghana.
NAM now has 120 member countries, 17 observer states and 10 international organisations, and has become more economic than political.
Non-alignment did not mean neutrality or demilitarisation, but independence of decision, and the policy remains in force.

problem.en: What is non-alignment and why did India choose it?

text.en: It means not joining any military bloc, and judging issues independently.

why.en: The Cold War had split the world into US and Soviet camps.

text.en: Nehru wanted to protect India's independence and focus on development.

why.en: Newly free nations could not afford military entanglements.

text.en: It did not mean neutrality or isolation.

why.en: India still made friends and defended itself.

prompt.en: List the objectives and determinants of foreign policy.

requiredIdeas.en: Friendly nations, world peace, economic development
Geography, history, resources, military strength, international milieu

commonMisconceptions.en: Saying non-alignment meant staying neutral in all disputes

points.en: Foreign policy protects national interests; Article 51 sets principles.
Non-alignment: no military blocs, independent decisions.
NAM founders: Nehru, Tito, Nasser, Sukarno, Nkrumah.
